You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:

- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
On the last day of the lost property office, someone came in for the piano.

Ruth had expected the umbrellas to go first. Rain was working its way through the station roof, and she’d propped the door open with a box of paperbacks and put out a sign: TAKE WHAT YOU CAN USE. By eleven, someone had taken the box.

The man who wanted the piano was wearing bicycle clips. He said his name was Daniel, and when Ruth asked if the piano was his, he said, “No, but I’ve got a receipt.”

The receipt was from a café that had closed nine years earlier. On the back, in blue ballpoint, someone had written: *If you ever find a piano, you owe me one.*

“Who wrote that?” Ruth asked.

“My sister.”

“Did you lose her piano?”

“I pushed it down a hill.”

Ruth waited. People often improved their stories if you gave them a moment.

“We were moving it,” he said. “I was in charge of the bottom end.”

The piano had arrived at the station during the renovation of the waiting room. In the paperwork it was listed as a package, dimensions unknown. It had taken four men to get it into the office, where it was immediately put to work supporting a microwave. Now a red sticker on the lid said it was to be collected on Monday for disposal.

“You’ll need a van,” Ruth said.

Daniel looked out at his bicycle. “I thought I might.”

He went away to make a call, and Ruth ate a pear over the wastebasket. Her daughter had offered to come down and help her clear the office, but Ruth had said there was nothing to clear. This was the kind of thing she said to her daughter and then spent an afternoon making true.

At noon a woman came in to ask where lost things would go after today.

“There’s a form online,” Ruth told her.

“But where do the things go?”

Ruth had been to the depot. It was a windowless building beside a roundabout, and to visit it by public transport you had to take a bus whose driver sometimes forgot there was a stop. She gave the woman the address.

“I haven’t lost anything,” the woman said. “I just thought I ought to know.”

A little after two, Daniel returned with a van and his sister. His sister was called Helen and had the receipt in her hand. She laid it on the counter and looked at Ruth.

“He told you about the hill, did he?”

“He said he was at the bottom end.”

“He was at the top. I was at the bottom. That’s why I’m still so cross.”

She took off her raincoat. Daniel went back out to find somewhere the van could stay without blocking the bus.

Ruth moved the microwave to the floor. Helen lifted the lid and played several notes, then the same notes harder, as if the piano might not have heard her the first time.

“Is it awful?” Ruth asked.

“Parts of it.”

She played something Ruth knew well enough to notice when Helen went wrong. Her father used to play it on Sundays, after lunch, with his belt undone by one notch. Halfway through, he would usually stop and ask whether anybody wanted a cup of tea. If nobody did, he made one anyway. Ruth realized she didn’t know how the piece ended.

Daniel came back. There was nowhere for the van. A bus was waiting, and its driver had got out.

“Just a minute,” Helen said.

The driver appeared in the doorway. Ruth knew him slightly. He’d lost a glove in February and had come in three times to see if she had it, each time taking the remaining glove from his pocket to show her. Now he stood with his hands at his sides until Helen finished. The last few notes were nothing like what Ruth had expected. There was a little descending run, then a pause long enough for her to think it was over, then one more note, quite low.

“Ten minutes,” the driver said. “I’ll go round the other way.”

They got the piano as far as the threshold before one of the front wheels came off. Daniel went to look for a brick. Ruth knelt and put her fingers under the corner, then took them out again. Years ago a porter had shown her how to move a filing cabinet alone. She could remember the porter’s wristwatch, which had a hairline crack across the face, but not what he’d done with the cabinet.

Her phone rang. It was her daughter, asking if she was home yet.

“No,” Ruth said. “I could use a hand, actually.”

“All right,” her daughter said. “I’ve got the kids.”

“Bring them.”

Daniel came back with half a brick. Helen told him not to put it there, and he asked where he should put it, and she said she didn’t know yet, but not there. Ruth went out to the platform so her daughter could hear her.

The rain had stopped. Across the tracks, a man on the far platform was walking briskly toward the footbridge, carrying a long yellow umbrella. Ruth recognized it by the black tape around the handle. It had been in the office since before Christmas.

He’d nearly reached the stairs when he stopped and looked up at the sky. Then he doubled back a few steps and put the umbrella on a bench, well in from the edge so it wouldn’t fall. He checked the clock and ran for his train.

Ruth watched the umbrella until her daughter said, “Mum? Which entrance?”

“The side one,” Ruth said, and went to prop it open.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet literary story built around a closing lost property office, with gently comic dialogue and a tender, understated resolution.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and dryly amused, but its humor makes room for grief and affection rather than deflecting them. Ruth’s small acts—holding the door, calling her daughter, noticing the umbrella—carry the story’s emotional weight; she is a person who often claims there is nothing to do, then finds herself doing it. The piano draws family memory into the present, while the ending turns a lost object into a choice to keep the door open. The reader is invited to notice care in unceremonious gestures, and to accept that an ending can also make space for someone to arrive.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds lost and recovered things: the piano, the umbrella, the glove, and even the remembered piece of music that Ruth cannot recall to its ending. Rain, stations, thresholds, and practical interruptions give the setting a mood of ordinary endings. Its moral emphasis is quiet: attention and help matter, even when no one makes a speech about them.

## Evidence line
This was the kind of thing she said to her daughter and then spent an afternoon making true.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring lost objects, understated humor, and small gestures of care make the sample distinctive and coherent evidence of a preference for quiet, emotionally indirect storytelling.
